problem: Earlier real-world 3D indoor scan datasets used for embodied AI are either small or low quality. Matterport3D has 90 scenes. Gibson has 571 scenes, but only 106 are rated acceptable quality. ScanNet and Replica are mostly room-scale. Many of these scans have holes, missing surfaces or untextured regions, which let agents 'see through walls'. This caps the scale and realism available for training navigation agents.
motivation: Embodied agents are trained in simulators on reconstructed scenes, so the scale, completeness and visual fidelity of those scenes limit how well agents generalize. The data-scaling hypothesis is well established for passive perception but untested for embodied perception, because no large, high-quality 3D dataset existed. The authors release 1,000 curated building-scale Matterport scans, packaged for Habitat, to fill this gap and test that hypothesis.
key_idea: Curate and release 1,000 near-complete, high-fidelity, building-scale Matterport reconstructions (HM3D) packaged for Habitat, and show that PointNav agents trained on them match or beat agents trained on any other dataset, whichever dataset they are tested on.
insight: Total navigable area in the training scenes is the dominant factor in PointNav performance. SPL scales nearly linearly with navigable area (Pearson ρ = 0.88 across HM3D 10%/50%/100% and the other datasets, Fig. 8; 0.82–0.97 per val set in Table A2). The train–val mismatch in episode difficulty (EMD of geodesic-distance histograms) is negatively correlated with SPL (about −0.4 to −0.7 on MP3D/HM3D val). In contrast, visual fidelity (KID, −0.30 to +0.1) and % reconstruction defects are only weakly correlated or uncorrelated with in-simulation SPL. So HM3D's benefit for sim PointNav comes mainly from scale and layout diversity rather than photorealism; the authors caveat that fidelity may still matter for sim-to-real.
method: Scene curation: 1,000 scenes were selected from a larger pool of Matterport Pro2 scans from 38 countries and 181 regions. 15 volunteer annotators rated each scene 1-5 for holes/cracks, furnishing, closed doors, interactive potential and navigability metrics. 3 expert annotators then picked highly ranked scenes while preserving diversity in floor count. Personal information was blurred before meshing; the effort was 800+ human hours.

Scale metrics: floor area (2D convex hull of navigable points per floor, as in Gibson), navigable area (Habitat navmesh for a 0.1 m radius, 1.5 m tall robot), navigation complexity (max geodesic/Euclidean ratio) and scene clutter (mesh area within 0.5 m of navigable space divided by navigable area). HM3D has 365.42k m² floor area and 112.50k m² navigable area.

View-based completeness ('% defects') metric: navigable space is gridded into 1 m cells and 4 headings are rendered per cell as 256×256, 90° FoV RGB-D views. A view counts as defective if more than 5% of its depth pixels are 0 or more than 5% of its RGB pixels are pure black; the scene score is the fraction of defective views.
Visual fidelity metric: FID/KID of rendered views against real RGB crops from the Gibson and MP3D raw panoramas.

PointNav benchmark splits: HM3D is split into 800 train / 100 val / 100 test scenes, with 8.0M train / 2,500 val / 2,500 test episodes (10k per train scene, 25 per val/test scene) generated with the Habitat script. The authors also generate 4.11M episodes for full Gibson train.

Agent benchmarking: the standard DD-PPO PointNav-v1 agent (ResNet-50 with GroupNorm, GPS+compass MLP, 2-layer 512-d LSTM, actor-critic heads) is trained for 1.5B frames on each of Gibson 4+, Gibson, MP3D and HM3D. Separate depth-only and RGB-only agents are trained, and each is cross-evaluated on the Gibson, MP3D and HM3D val/test sets. Data scaling is probed with HM3D 10% (80 scenes) and 50% (400 scenes) subsets.

numbers_note: This is a dataset paper; the 'own method' is the standard DD-PPO PointNav agent trained on HM3D. The paper prints Success and SPL as fractions (e.g., 0.93), converted here to 0-100. The HM3D 10% / 50% scaling agents are shown only in Figure 8 (SPL vs navigable area) with no numeric table; learning curves are in Figure 6 and the SPL-vs-difficulty plot in Figure 7. Dataset-quality numbers are also reported but are not navigation metrics: FID/KID vs Gibson real 20.5 / 15.8±1.0 and vs MP3D real 20.5 / 12.8±0.8 (Fig. 5b), plus Table 1 scale stats.
results: HM3D-trained PointNav agents are best or tied-best on every test set ('pareto-optimal'). With depth input they reach SR 1.00 / SPL 0.93 on Gibson test, which ties the in-domain Gibson agent (1.00 / 0.94). They reach 0.94 / 0.83 on MP3D test versus the next-best Gibson agent's 0.90 / 0.80, and 0.99 / 0.92 on HM3D test. With RGB input they reach 1.00 / 0.90 on Gibson, 0.85 / 0.71 on MP3D (Gibson agent: 0.82 / 0.68) and 0.98 / 0.87 on HM3D. As a dataset, HM3D has 1.4–3.7× more navigable area (112.5k m²) than prior datasets and 20–85% better FID vs real images. It has more than 3× as many scenes with under 5% defective views as Gibson (560 vs 175).
limitations: At release there are no semantic annotations; HM3D supports only geometric tasks (e.g., PointNav) in static environments. ObjectNav and rearrangement were deferred to future semantic extensions.
Geographic and socioeconomic bias: scans come only from owners of the roughly $3k Matterport Pro2 with internet access, in 38 countries.

Downstream validation covers only PointNav in simulation, with 1 training seed and no real-robot transfer. Near-saturated Gibson results limit how discriminative the comparison is, and the Gibson depth agent still has slightly higher SPL on Gibson test (0.94 vs 0.93).
